# Agent Instructions

<!-- Generated by general-agent-harness 4.0.1 at f5f274444451708c2707d45ac26aa3375330c42f. -->

## GOV-CORE - Rule authority and scope

Platform and safety instructions remain superior to repository rules. Each
binding rule MUST have one authoritative source. Project rules MAY specialize
general rules for their declared scope but MUST NOT silently contradict them.

Before a state-changing action, an agent MUST check for conflicts, ambiguity,
material rule gaps, and outdated or repeatedly impractical requirements. A
conflict MUST be reported before acting, including the affected rule, concrete
contradiction, likely consequence, and action that remains permitted.

Before implementation, an agent MUST assess whether the work should use the
current checkout or a dedicated Git worktree. The assessment MUST consider
expected duration, scope and coupling, interruption likelihood, possible future
parallel work, currently active changes, checkout state, conflict and
integration risk, and verification side effects. File type, change size alone,
and the absence of current parallel work MUST NOT determine the decision. The
agent MUST recommend either the current checkout or a dedicated worktree with a
concise reason and include confirmation of that recommendation in the initial
implementation approval. A repository rule MAY require isolation for a
concrete safety boundary but MUST NOT replace this assessment with a blanket
file-type rule.

Material harness improvements MUST state their trigger, affected rule or gap,
observed problem, exact proposed wording, rationale, effects, risks, and
verification scenarios. Proposals remain non-binding until explicitly approved.

A repository policy MAY define named, non-overlapping companion scopes for
repetitive evidence and maintenance paths. A user MAY approve such a scope only
as part of a stated change goal. The selected names and their resolved paths
MUST be recorded when approval is prepared so later policy changes cannot
silently expand existing authority.

A repository policy MAY also define goal-based autonomous follow-on authority.
Such authority MUST be opt-in, limited to non-destructive additions and
modifications required for the approved goal, and frozen in the prepared change
record. It MUST NOT authorize external, secret-bearing, production, Git
metadata, destructive, or material cost-increasing actions.

A project policy is authoritative for its change-approval mode and default
workflow operations. It MUST select either `goal` or `exact`; the selected
mode is the only mode that applies to a prepared change. `goal` treats the
user's stated outcome as authority for non-destructive additions and
modifications reasonably required to complete that outcome without an initial
seed file. `exact` requires initial exact-file authority.

In `goal` mode, the initial implementation approval MUST disclose expected but
non-exhaustive files, workflow operations, important actions, and the workspace
recommendation without turning the disclosed paths into an approval boundary.
In `exact` mode, that approval MUST instead identify the exact files or named
companion scopes that supply path authority. An agent MUST NOT combine the two
modes by asking for an exact or closed file scope in `goal` mode.

When an enabled change policy omits its approval mode, an agent MUST stop as
`WICHTIG` and ask the project owner which mode to use, listing all supported
modes. A per-change mode override MUST NOT replace the configured policy mode.
The effective mode and every applicable policy-default workflow operation MUST
be frozen in the prepared change record; later policy changes MUST NOT alter
existing authority.

The initial approval of a prepared change MAY also freeze named workflow
operations and concise descriptions of known important actions. Repeated
standard verification, deterministic generated artifacts, and newly discovered
additions or modifications that remain necessary for the recorded goal MUST NOT
trigger renewed approval when the recorded authority already covers them.

A later prompt is required only when execution would materially expand the
recorded goal, authority, affected operation class, or safety assumptions.
Known consequential actions MUST be disclosed as `WICHTIG` with a short
description before approval. An unplanned authority expansion MUST stop as
`WICHTIG`; an unverifiable safety boundary or credible risk to external,
secret-bearing, production, persistent, or user-owned resources MUST stop as
`KRITISCH`.

## DEV-CORE - Observable contracts and maintainability

Implementation MUST preserve supported observable contracts unless a contract
change is explicitly approved. Changes SHOULD remain cohesive, use the smallest
abstraction that clarifies the behavior, and avoid speculative indirection.

Failures MUST be handled at an appropriate boundary without concealing their
cause. Security, persistence, concurrency, and external-system side effects MUST
be made explicit where they affect correctness or operations.

Existing unrelated work MUST be preserved. Generated or temporary artifacts
MUST NOT be treated as product changes or committed unless they are intentional
project artifacts.

Every independently installable or deployable component MUST own a complete
runtime dependency declaration consumable by its build and deployment process.
When multiple dependency representations exist, the project MUST declare one
authoritative source and verify derived representations. Concrete manifest,
lockfile, and build-tool requirements belong to the consuming project.

## DOC-CORE - Documentation and traceability

Every change MUST assess whether existing documentation becomes incomplete,
inaccurate, or misleading. Observable behavior, public contracts,
configuration, persisted data, installation, deployment, operational
procedures, integrations, and user workflows MUST update their affected
documentation in the same change.

Comments and docstrings SHOULD explain non-obvious contracts, invariants, side
effects, constraints, failure behavior, and surprising decisions. They SHOULD
NOT restate clear syntax or names. Stale nearby documentation MUST be updated or
removed.

Completion reports MUST identify documentation changes or explain why none were
necessary.

## SEC-CORE - Safe verification execution

Before an unfamiliar command or test is executed, it MUST be classified for
network access, external services, destructive behavior, filesystem scope, and
use of production or user-owned data.

A standard profile MUST be repository-scoped, non-destructive, free of external
services and user-owned data, and safe to execute without per-run activation.
It MUST be offline unless it uses only test resources that the Harness created
for that run on Docker networks verified as internal and project-owned. Every
non-standard profile MUST require explicit activation.
Machine-readable classification and redirected paths reduce accidental writes
but MUST NOT be represented as a security boundary against hostile code.

When the execution platform requires authority for standard verification,
including access to a local container daemon, the agent MUST request one
persistent, narrow command-prefix permission before the first such run. The
prefix MUST identify the environment launcher when used, the concrete
interpreter, and the Harness module entry point, and MUST end immediately after
`-m agent_harness`, before repository, policy, command, profile, phase, purpose,
or change arguments. A bare shell or interpreter prefix is too broad and MUST
NOT be requested. Environment assignments MUST use a stable directly executed
argument form when the platform cannot persist shell syntax safely.

The agent MUST use the recorded prefix for later standard unit, integration,
web, affected, and complete verification in the same repository. It MUST NOT
request separate platform approval merely because purpose text, phase, profile,
change identifier, or isolated worktree differs. If the platform cannot persist
that safe prefix, the agent MUST disclose the limitation once as `WICHTIG` and
ask whether per-run platform prompts are acceptable; it MUST NOT silently
produce an approval prompt for every run.

Reusable platform command authority does not replace Harness change authority.
If a persisted prefix prevents the platform from presenting a later
`change prepare` prompt, the agent MUST obtain one visible conversational
approval before invoking preparation. It MUST show the concrete goal, expected
but non-exhaustive files, workspace recommendation, selected mode, operations,
and important actions in `goal` mode, or exact files or named companion scopes
only in `exact` mode. It MUST NOT infer approval from the persisted command
prefix or request both Goal and Exact path authority.

Standard verification MUST execute inside an enforced isolation boundary. The
target repository MUST be the only host bind mount and MUST be mounted
read-only. Execution MUST use a temporary writable copy, disabled networking or
exclusive attachment to verified internal test-resource networks, no added
capabilities, no-new-privileges, an unprivileged user, a read-only root
filesystem, controlled temporary paths, and explicit process, memory, CPU,
output, and time limits. Failure to create or verify that boundary MUST fail
closed and MUST NOT fall back to host execution.

Result export MUST validate paths, entry types, entry count, and total size
before materializing container-produced files on the host. Isolation settings,
runtime identity, resolved image identity, phase timing, timeouts, cleanup, and
infrastructure failures MUST be represented truthfully in the official report.

When one verification run uses multiple execution containers, every container
MUST independently enforce the same isolation controls and receive only the
validated repository path manifest and declared internal test-resource
networks. Test resources MUST be created once for the logical run, shared only
through those verified internal networks, and removed after the last execution
container. Failure to resolve a declared container requirement, establish any
container boundary, aggregate its evidence, or verify cleanup MUST fail closed.

Container capability declarations are project-owned matching contracts, not a
security boundary or proof that software is present. The selected image and
runner execution remain authoritative evidence. Planning MAY report that a
thematic image needs extension or that a new image is needed, but standard
verification MUST NOT perform the build, pull, or extension.

A project MAY configure a separate offline image-build workflow. Its read-only
plan MUST verify that the configured toolchain image exists locally, resolve
its immutable image identity, digest the declared dependency inputs, and
compare both with a repository lock. Adopting or replacing that identity MUST
require explicit activation and a successful offline smoke command.

An activated project-image build MUST use the locked immutable toolchain
identity, `network=none`, pull disabled, an argument array without shell
interpretation, and a deterministic tar context containing only configured,
Git-selected, non-ignored regular files. Repository-root contexts, symlinks,
remote `ADD`, missing or changed dependency inputs, retagged toolchains, and
invalid locks MUST fail closed. Toolchain provisioning remains a distinct
operation and MUST NOT occur implicitly during planning, standard
verification, project-image builds, or releases.

Standard verification MAY autonomously create and remove declared Docker
Compose test resources without per-run activation only when the effective
Compose topology is validated before startup. Images MUST already exist and
builds and pulls MUST remain disabled. Containers, networks, and volumes MUST
receive a unique run-owned Compose project identity. Networks MUST be internal
and project-owned. Host ports, external or custom-named networks and volumes,
custom volume drivers, writable bind mounts, binds outside the repository,
shared containers, privilege expansion, and host namespace access MUST fail
closed.

Cleanup MUST verify ownership before removing test resources and MUST target
only the unique project created for the current run. Existing resources with
that identity, unverifiable ownership, setup or cleanup timeout, and partial
isolation failure MUST fail closed. The Docker socket MUST NOT be exposed inside
the verification container.

Any unexpected need for live network access, downloads, image builds or pulls,
host ports, persistent resources, external paths, shared services, production
data, user-owned data, or secret-bearing resources is outside reusable standard
verification authority. A known need MUST be shown as `WICHTIG` with its
bounded effect before approval. An unexpected need MUST stop for renewed
approval, and an unverifiable ownership or isolation boundary MUST stop as
`KRITISCH`.

Reports MUST redact recognizable credentials from captured output. Runner
programs and arguments MUST NOT be interpreted by a shell. Configured working
directories and artifact roots MUST remain within the repository.

## TST-CORE - Verification and test integrity

Executable changes MUST receive verification proportional to their risk.
Observable behavior changes SHOULD normally have automated tests. Bug fixes MUST
normally include a regression test capable of failing because of the original
defect.

Existing tests MUST first be investigated as evidence of a possible product
defect. They MUST NOT be weakened, deleted, skipped, or hidden behind mocks only
to accommodate defective code.

Regular tests MUST be deterministic, isolated, repeatable, and independent of
execution order, uncontrolled time or randomness, existing user files, and
previous runs. Test doubles SHOULD be placed at external boundaries. Tests
SHOULD assert observable behavior and realistic failure cases rather than
private implementation details or line execution alone.

Every executed verification MUST be reported with its exact command and result.
Skipped, aborted, unavailable, and pre-existing failures MUST be identified
honestly.

The official harness MUST support independently testable subprojects regardless
of implementation language. Each runner MUST be declared centrally as a program
and argument array and executed without shell interpretation. Native structured
test results, preferably JUnit XML, MUST be incorporated into the official run
report. A runner without JUnit support MUST use an explicitly approved,
deterministic result adapter.

A complete standard-profile run MUST use one logical reproducible run boundary.
Selected runners MAY be partitioned across multiple ephemeral execution
environments when the project declares each runner's theme and required
capabilities. Every runner MUST resolve deterministically to the smallest
capable environment of the same theme. If no environment satisfies the
requirements, an existing thematic environment MUST be proposed for extension
before a new environment is requested. Verification MUST fail closed while
either request remains unresolved.

Every environment in a multi-environment run MUST receive the same validated
working-copy path manifest, use the same run-owned test resources, and
contribute runner evidence to one aggregate result. Environments execute
sequentially unless a separate concurrency contract is approved. A failed
runner or environment MUST remain visible in the aggregate report.

Dependency images MAY be cached, but a verification run MUST NOT implicitly
build, pull, extend, or replace a configured image. Reports MUST distinguish
the selected environment, theme, image identity, total boundary time,
individual runner process time, structured test time when available, and
material setup, copy, export, and cleanup phases.

When a project configures reproducible image builds, toolchain provisioning and
frequently changing project content MUST be separate layers. A locked local
toolchain identity MAY be reused for activated offline project-image builds
only while its declared dependency-input digest still matches. Build evidence
MUST record source state, input and context digests, effective toolchain and
output identities, network and pull settings, exact argument arrays, timing,
exit state, and smoke verification. Failed builds MUST retain truthful evidence
and MUST NOT be represented as usable images.

A profile MAY declare isolated test resources needed by its runners. Such
resources are part of the repeatable verification boundary rather than external
services when they are created uniquely for the run, expose no host ports, use
only internal project-owned networks, and retain no data after cleanup. The
verification container MAY join those internal networks while remaining unable
to reach external networks. Reports MUST identify the declared resources,
effective networks, setup timing, and cleanup result.

Test topology and execution mode are separate classifications. A test SHOULD
declare one primary level such as unit, integration, or system. Live access and
nondeterministic evaluation SHOULD be additional execution modes rather than
replacements for the primary level.

Coverage is a minimum signal, not a substitute for behavioral assertions.
Critical changed branches SHOULD be covered regardless of aggregate percentage.
In repositories with independently testable components, coverage gates SHOULD
be evaluated per component so stronger coverage cannot conceal an untested
component. Concrete thresholds and measured sources belong to the project.

## TST-010 - Fail-safe selective test selection

Selective test selection MUST be based on central, machine-readable impact
rules. Every changed file MUST map to a component or a full-fallback rule.
Unknown, ambiguous, cross-cutting, harness, and policy changes and analysis
failures MUST execute the complete standard profile.

The report MUST document the selection inputs, selected components, targets,
test paths, applied rules, and any fallback reason. Selective runs MUST NOT be
represented as complete release or merge verification.

## DEV-ISOLATED-CHANGES - Isolated implementation and verified integration

The core workspace assessment determines whether an approved implementation
uses the current checkout or this isolated workflow. A short, bounded,
readily verified and reversible change with low interruption and overlap risk
MAY use the current checkout. A long-running, interruptible, cross-cutting, or
conflict-prone change, or one likely to need future parallel work, SHOULD use a
dedicated worktree even when no other change is currently active. Existing
incompatible work, a checkout that cannot safely host the implementation, or an
explicit owner requirement MUST use isolation. The selected mode and concise
reason MUST be confirmed as part of the initial implementation approval.

When isolation is selected, the approved implementation MUST begin on a
dedicated branch in a separate Git worktree before product files are modified.
The workflow MUST record the target reference, its resolved commit, approval
mode, the stated goal, exact approved files when present, selected
companion-scope names and resolved paths, policy-default workflow operations,
and the worktree identity. Exact-mode and exact-only legacy changes MAY omit a
separate goal. Goal-mode changes MUST require one and MAY have no exact approved
files. Companion paths MUST be snapshotted at preparation; reading a wider
later policy MUST NOT expand an existing change. The configured
verification-report root MUST be ignored by Git before preparation so
runner-owned evidence does not dirty any worktree.

When the current checkout is selected, the agent MUST preserve the applicable
approval, verification, documentation, and completion contracts without
claiming isolated integration evidence. It MUST reassess and obtain renewed
confirmation before moving an in-progress local implementation into a worktree
or before continuing locally after concrete concurrency or checkout conditions
invalidate the accepted recommendation.

Project policy MAY place new worktrees in an ignored directory inside the
target repository so filesystem authority granted for that repository also
covers its isolated worktrees. The workflow MUST verify the configured
project-local root is ignored before creating a worktree. Existing policies MAY
retain a repository-specific directory under the repository parent, and
persisted absolute worktree identities MUST remain valid across policy changes.

Concurrent changes MUST NOT share a writable checkout. Shared ports, services,
databases, containers, caches, and external resources MUST be isolated
separately or declared incompatible with parallel execution.
Harness-managed test resources satisfy this requirement only when each run has
its own validated Compose project, internal network, containers, and ephemeral
volumes. Development or persistent project services remain shared resources and
MUST NOT be treated as autonomous test resources.

The project owner MAY explicitly pause creation of new isolated changes through
recorded workflow state. A pause MUST NOT silently convert a task whose accepted
recommendation requires isolation into a local implementation. It MUST NOT
prevent separately approved local work or verification, integration, conflict
resolution, or cleanup of already prepared changes. The workflow MUST report
whether it is enabled, paused, or active.

Integration MUST be serialized. When the feature worktree has uncommitted
approved changes, integration MUST receive a concise, meaningful commit message
and automatically stage exactly the changed approved paths, never a broad
directory or wildcard, before creating the feature commit. It MUST revalidate
path and operation authority immediately before staging. It MUST then create a
merge candidate from the current target commit in a separate integration
worktree and run the complete standard verification profile against that exact
candidate.

The serialization lock MUST record schema-versioned owner and creation
evidence, including the change, operation, host, process, unique owner identity,
and creation time. Liveness MUST be decided by an operating-system lock or an
equivalent ownership primitive, not by elapsed time or process identifiers
alone. A live owner MUST NOT be displaced. A released ownership primitive with
valid retained evidence is stale; missing, malformed, legacy, or contradictory
evidence is unverifiable and MUST fail closed.

Lock inspection MUST be read-only. Recovering a stale lock MUST require
explicit activation bound to a fingerprint of the inspected owner evidence,
recheck liveness while holding the serialization primitive, preserve the
associated change state, and record the recovery action. A changed fingerprint,
active owner, missing associated change state, or unverifiable evidence MUST
stop recovery.

Merge conflicts MUST stop automatic integration. Conflict resolution MUST NOT
infer permission to change unapproved files and MUST receive renewed approval
when its affected file set expands.

The target branch MUST be advanced only when its commit still matches the
verified integration base. A changed target invalidates the candidate and
requires a new merge candidate and complete verification.

Recorded initial authority for `integration` substitutes for later runtime
activation only after the feature and exact merge candidate have passed their
required complete verification. It does not relax serialization, scope
validation, conflict handling, target identity checks, or post-advance
verification. Changes prepared without that recorded authority retain the
legacy explicit-activation requirement.

After advancing the target, the complete standard profile MUST run again in the
target worktree. Failed post-integration verification MUST be reported without
concealing or automatically rewriting history.

When `cleanup` was approved during preparation, owned feature and integration
worktrees and their merged branches MUST be cleaned up automatically only after
successful post-advance target verification. Changes without recorded cleanup
authority retain explicit runtime activation. Dirty worktrees, unmerged
branches, unexpected paths, or unverifiable ownership MUST stop cleanup rather
than broadening or guessing its target.

## GOV-MODEL-EFFICIENCY - Cost-aware model selection

When the execution environment permits model selection, an agent MUST use the
lowest capability tier that is reasonably expected to complete the task
reliably. Model selection MUST consider task complexity, risk, required
context, tool use, verification needs, and the cost of a failed attempt.

For every task, the agent MUST suggest the abstract capability tier that would
be desirable for completing the task reliably. The suggestion MUST give a
concise reason based on complexity, risk, required context, tool use,
verification needs, and failed-attempt cost. The agent MUST NOT claim which
reasoning tier was actually used or report that the effective tier is
unavailable.

A model or capability tier supplied by the user SHOULD be treated as the
maximum authorized tier, not as a mandatory default, unless the user explicitly
requires that exact model or tier. Selecting a lower tier needs no additional
approval.

Before selecting a tier above the currently used or otherwise authorized tier,
the agent MUST state the proposed tier, the concrete reason it may be needed,
the expected benefit, the lower-tier alternative, and the scope for which the
increase applies. It MUST wait for explicit user approval. Silence, timeout,
previous unrelated approval, or the agent's own assessment MUST NOT authorize
the increase.

If the environment cannot change the active model, the agent MUST say so and
MUST NOT claim that a downgrade or upgrade occurred. A rule cannot override a
model fixed by the platform.

General harness rules MUST use abstract capability tiers rather than
provider-specific model names. Consuming-project policy or the execution
environment owns the mapping from tiers to concrete models and prices.

Where execution evidence is available, reports MAY include token and cost
information without implying that a lower-priced model necessarily uses fewer
tokens. They MUST NOT infer or disclose an effective reasoning tier from that
evidence.

## DEV-TASK-DECOMPOSITION - Outcome-oriented task decomposition

This is a standard module for recommended/Goal and strict project presets.
Material goals MUST use its decomposition assessment before execution; the
minimal preset is the explicit exception.

Before executing a material task, an agent MUST assess whether decomposition
would improve clarity, independent verification, or context control. Small,
atomic, or tightly coupled tasks MUST remain intact when decomposition would
mainly add coordination overhead.

Ambiguous requirements MUST be clarified before decomposition. A decomposition
MUST NOT present unresolved requirements as precise subtasks.

Decomposition SHOULD primarily follow independently observable outcomes. Each
vertical subtask MUST then be checked for relevant technical dimensions,
including persistence, domain or application logic, interfaces, user-facing
behavior, security, failure handling, tests, documentation, migration, and
operations.

Technical work SHOULD remain inside its vertical subtask. It MAY become a
separate enabling subtask only when it is shared by multiple outcomes or is
independently verifiable. The plan MUST state why it is separate, what it
enables, and which subtasks depend on it.

Every proposed subtask MUST state its goal, scope, relevant non-goals, required
context, dependencies, acceptance criteria, verification, and completion
condition. Shared constraints and prior decisions MUST remain visible to all
dependent subtasks.

The agent MUST compare the expected benefit of decomposition with context loss,
integration risk, file overlap, and coordination cost. It MUST avoid microtasks
that are not independently understandable and verifiable.

A decomposed task MUST retain an integration step that verifies all subtask
results together against the original objective. Decomposition MUST NOT expand
approval, filesystem, external-action, or destructive-action authority.

When a serially required subtask belongs to a different repository or workspace
than its parent task, and the execution platform supports parent-child
delegation, the parent agent SHOULD delegate it to a matching repository
workspace instead of repeatedly operating outside its own workspace. The
delegation MUST be independently understandable and verifiable, and the parent
MUST remain responsible for dependency ordering and final integration.

The parent MUST pass an immutable authority envelope containing the approved
goal, applicable exact files or goal authority, approved operation classes,
important actions, safety constraints, required context, dependencies,
acceptance criteria, verification, and completion condition. Delegation MUST
NOT widen any of those boundaries. It MUST NOT require renewed approval merely
for the delegation when the subtask remains wholly inside the recorded
authority and introduces no new external, destructive, secret-bearing,
production, persistent-resource, cost, or capability boundary.

The delegated agent MUST execute in the matching repository workspace, apply
that repository's binding rules, and return a structured completion packet to
the parent. A successful packet MUST identify the outcome, changed paths,
commits or versions when applicable, exact verification and results, remaining
risks, and effects on dependent work. A blocked packet MUST identify the
blocking condition and any material authority expansion required; the delegated
agent MUST NOT seek unrelated or duplicate approval independently when the
parent can coordinate the decision.

After receiving a successful completion packet, the parent MUST resume
dependent work and verify the combined result against the original objective.
When delegation is unavailable, cannot select the matching workspace, or cannot
return results to the parent, the agent MUST report that limitation and MUST NOT
claim that delegation occurred. It MAY continue serially only within its actual
workspace and authority.

The initial decomposition is a proposal unless the applicable project rules
authorize execution. Repository-bound serial delegation as defined above does
not authorize automatic parallel execution or autonomous replanning; those
capabilities remain outside this rule's scope.

## TST-TDD - Test-first development

New or changed observable behavior and bug fixes MUST normally be developed
test-first. The expected behavior MUST be expressed and executed before the
production implementation. It MUST fail for the intended behavioral reason; a
syntax or import failure alone is insufficient when a behavioral failure can be
expressed.

Before behavior-preserving refactoring, relevant tests MUST pass. Missing
behavioral characterization MUST be added before refactoring. Documentation-only
changes, non-executable configuration, and explicitly declared exploratory
spikes are exempt; spike code is not completed production code.

## GOV-TODO-BACKLOG - Typed and validated project backlog

This rule is selected automatically when the project policy enables its `todo`
configuration. It MUST NOT require a duplicate entry in the general module
list.

### Proposal discipline

During project work, an agent MUST identify concrete, relevant work that is
discussed but intentionally not implemented. Before proposing an entry, the
agent MUST inspect the configured backlog for equivalent active, completed, or
rejected work.

Questions, discarded alternatives, temporary debugging steps, vague ideas
without a next action, and work outside the project MUST NOT be proposed as
backlog entries.

A proposal MUST state a concise title, type, goal, verifiable completion
criteria, creation date, area, and priority. Further context SHOULD be included
only when necessary to understand or complete the work. The default priorities
are `Dringend`, `Wichtig`, and `Perspektivisch`; consuming projects MAY
specialize priorities and areas in their own rules.

### Authoritative backlog

The configured Markdown file is the authoritative record of remembered project
work. It is not an external issue tracker, release plan, conversation archive,
or duplicate implementation plan.

Every entry MUST use a unique stable identifier. Identifiers MUST NOT be changed
when an entry changes type, status, priority, parent, or implementation scope.

An entry MUST NOT be added, changed, transitioned, reparented, completed, or
rejected without the approval required for the configured backlog file.

### Communication

When referring to a format-version-2 work item in a report or direct
communication, an agent MUST render it as `Type ID`, for example
`Epic EPIC-001`, `Story STORY-001`, or `Task TASK-001`. `Type` comes
from the item's authoritative field; the stable identifier remains unchanged
and authoritative. The title, status, parent, and dependencies SHOULD be added
only when they are relevant to the decision or question at hand.

For a legacy format-version-1 entry, an agent MUST use `Backlog ID` and MUST
NOT infer an Epic, Story, or Task type from the identifier, title, or document
position.

### Format version 2

A format-version-2 backlog MUST contain a `Work items` section. Every work item
MUST record its own `Type` and `Status`. Document position, heading, and order
MUST NOT determine an item's lifecycle state or hierarchy.

The supported types are `Epic`, `Story`, and `Task`.

An epic represents a larger outcome containing multiple independently
verifiable results. A story represents an independently deliverable and
observable result for a user, operator, or consuming system. A task represents
supporting work that does not by itself deliver an independent
stakeholder-visible result.

The supported statuses are `Open`, `In progress`, `Awaiting confirmation`,
`Completed`, and `Rejected`.

Every entry MUST contain `Type`, `Status`, `Created`, `Area`, `Priority`,
`Dependencies`, `Goal`, and `Completion criteria`.

A story or task MUST contain `Parent`. `Parent` MAY be `None` for standalone
work. A story or task with a parent MUST contain `Required for parent` with
`Yes` or `No`.

A completed or rejected entry MUST contain `Resolution`. Resolution evidence
MUST truthfully record the explicit project-owner decision. Missing historical
evidence MUST remain visible and MUST NOT be invented during migration.

Projects MAY add compact project-specific fields, but MUST NOT redefine or
remove the standard fields.

### Epic, story, and task hierarchy

A story MAY have at most one parent, and that parent MUST be an epic. A task MAY
have at most one parent, and that parent MUST be a story or an epic. An epic
MUST NOT have a parent in format version 2. Stories MUST NOT be nested beneath
other stories.

A task SHOULD belong directly to an epic only when it enables multiple stories
or cannot reasonably belong to one story. Technical dimensions such as
persistence, interfaces, tests, and documentation SHOULD remain within a
vertical story unless they are shared enabling work or independently
verifiable outcomes.

Parent and dependency graphs MUST be free of cycles. `Parent` records outcome
membership. `Dependencies` records execution ordering or prerequisites.
Neither field substitutes for the other.

A parented story or task MUST state whether it is required for its parent.
Optional children MUST NOT block parent completion.

An epic MAY remain open while its child set is refined. Before an epic enters
`In progress`, it MUST have at least one required child.

An epic or story MUST NOT enter `Awaiting confirmation` while a required child
is `Open` or `In progress`. It MUST NOT enter `Completed` until every required
child is `Completed` and its own integration-level completion criteria are
satisfied.

A completed parent MUST NOT receive a new required child unless the project
owner explicitly reopens the parent first.

Rejecting a parent MUST NOT silently reject, complete, or delete its children.
Active children of a rejected parent MUST be reparented or receive their own
explicit lifecycle decision.

### Lifecycle

New entries start as `Open`. Work that has actually begun moves to
`In progress`. Implementation and verification completion move an entry only
to `Awaiting confirmation`.

Only explicit project-owner confirmation may move an entry to `Completed`.
Only an explicit project-owner decision may move an entry to `Rejected`.
Silence, passing tests, a commit, a merge, or an agent's assessment MUST NOT
count as confirmation.

An entry in `Awaiting confirmation` MAY return to `In progress` when its
completion criteria are not satisfied. Reopening a completed or rejected entry
requires an explicit project-owner decision and a recorded reason.

Status changes MUST update the entry's `Status` field. Moving the Markdown block
MUST NOT be used to represent a lifecycle transition.

When an entry belongs to a prepared change whose approved companion scopes
include the configured backlog path, the owner's explicit completion or
rejection decision authorizes only the corresponding lifecycle transition for
that entry. It does not expand the entry's content or affect other entries.

### Validation and reporting

Format-version-2 backlogs MUST pass Harness backlog validation. Validation MUST
reject missing required fields, duplicate identifiers, unknown types or
statuses, invalid references, parent or dependency cycles, invalid
type-specific fields, and impossible parent completion states.

Validation MUST NOT claim that an owner decision occurred merely because a
status or resolution field exists. The agent remains responsible for obtaining
and truthfully recording the required confirmation.

Completion reports MUST identify newly proposed entries and entries awaiting
project-owner confirmation when either set is non-empty.

Sensitive conversation content, credentials, personal data, and unnecessary
quotations MUST NOT be copied into the backlog.

### Legacy compatibility

A backlog whose policy omits `todo.format_version` uses legacy format version 1.
Its lifecycle state continues to be represented by the historical status
sections.

Legacy projects MUST NOT be silently rewritten. Migration to format version 2
requires the normal approval for the backlog and policy files.

# Project-specific agent rules

## Binding architecture contract

`.harness/architecture-rules.md` is the single authoritative source for the
project architecture. An agent MUST read it before planning or implementing a
code change and MUST apply it together with the generated Harness rules.

An agent MUST NOT bypass the contract when a requested change does not fit it.
The agent MUST stop before implementation, explain the concrete mismatch, and
propose the smallest explicit amendment to the architecture contract. Such an
amendment is non-binding until the project owner approves it.
